title: Samson (Judges 13–16)
hookLine: great strength, poor choices, and one last prayer

lines: NO RAZOR SHALL TOUCH HIS HEAD.
cards: A few days before Christmas, the weekday Mass reading sounds almost like a Gospel. A woman who has no children is visited by a messenger of God.
You will conceive and bear a son, he tells her, and no razor will touch his head; he'll be set apart for God from his mother's womb. That child grows up astonishingly strong.
He tears a lion apart with his hands and carries off a city's gates. And he makes one wrong choice after another. His name is Samson.

teach.h: A NAZARITE: SET APART FOR GOD.
teach.b: Samson is a Nazarite, Nazirite elsewhere: someone consecrated to God, who drinks no wine and never cuts his hair. The long hair is the sign of the vow; the strength is God's gift.
Keep those two apart, because Samson doesn't. He marries outside his people against his parents' pleading. He sets three hundred foxes loose with torches in the enemy's fields.
He's ruled by appetite and revenge. Then Delilah. Three times she asks what makes him strong, three times he lies, and three times the Philistines burst in.

The fourth time he tells her the truth, in the Douay-Rheims: "if my head be shaven, my strength shall depart from me." She lulls him to sleep on her knees, calls a barber, and his seven locks are shaved.

teach.h: THE LORD WAS DEPARTED FROM HIM.
teach.b: He wakes and thinks he'll shake himself free as before, "not knowing that the Lord was departed from him." The hair wasn't magic. Some readers see it as the last piece of a vow he had been bending all along.
Blinded and chained, he grinds grain in a prison, and his hair starts to grow.

At a feast for their god, they bring him out to mock him, and he prays: "O Lord God, remember me, and restore to me now my former strength." The rest of the prayer, the text admits, asks revenge for his eyes.
He pushes the pillars, and the house falls on him and on them. The Church doesn't hold Samson up as a model of virtue, but the Letter to the Hebrews names him among the people of faith.

teach.h: RESTORE TO ME NOW MY FORMER STRENGTH.
teach.b: Strength never made Samson wise. At the end, it was a prayer that made him remember who his strength belonged to.

how: Catholics hear the announcement of Samson's birth at daily Mass in late Advent, paired with the angel's announcement of John the Baptist's birth, and the Church reads his life as a warning as much as an example.

o: a judge given great strength, undone by his choices
a king of Israel well-known for his wise judgments
a Philistine giant defeated by young David

p: asked four times what made him strong

s: Samson told Delilah the truth the first time she asked
he lied three times, and the Philistines burst in three times, before he told her.
Samson thought his strength was still there when he woke
he didn't know that the Lord was departed from him.
the New Testament names Samson among people of faith
Hebrews 11:32 lists him with Gideon, Barak and Jephthah.

games.q: you're Samson. blind, chained, mocked at your enemies' feast, your hair just beginning to grow back. what do you do?
o: call on God to remember you.
games.why: he prays, "O Lord God, remember me," and pulls down the pillars. after a life of bad choices, his last act begins with a prayer.

practice: Samson's trouble wasn't a lack of strength but a soft spot he kept walking back into: flattery, anger, wanting what he wanted. Name yours quietly, and look at it the way you'd look at a door you keep leaving unlocked.
If you pray, borrow Samson's words, O Lord God, remember me; if not, just look, without excuses.

wordCard.voice: Samson. A judge consecrated to God from the womb, given great strength, who ruined much of it, and whose last act was a prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: nazir, the name for one under the vow. The vow is laid out in Numbers 6.

carryVoice: Your line: strength isn't wisdom. Samson had the one and not the other. Day three hundred ninety-four, done.
